blocks.text: A function returns an error, but the work may already have happened. A process is alive, but it cannot make progress. A second server appears, but it shares the first server’s storage and therefore its most important failure mode. A cache answers quickly, but with information old enough to invalidate the user’s decision. These are not problems that a more sophisticated pointer type can solve alone. They require an architecture that describes what each participant knows, which participant owns a fact, and what evidence justifies a successful response.

blocks.text: The recurring project is HarborDispatch, a fictional internal job-submission system. A client submits bounded work with a stable request key. A gateway records the intent in one database. A dispatcher sends it to a worker with a separate database. The worker records the operation’s result, and the gateway reconciles completion. The calculation is intentionally simple: square an integer in the documented range. Keeping the computation inspectable lets the book concentrate on request identity, duplicate delivery, crash recovery, overload, protocol evolution, and operational ownership.

topics.title: Audience and prerequisites
topics.summary: Readers should be comfortable with C++ classes, RAII, move semantics, containers, exceptions, basic concurrency, CMake, and the distinction between a process and a thread. Book IV’s systems material and Book V’s testing and build practices are the most direct preparation. GPU programming is not a prerequisite. This volume is about coordinating independently failing components, not about requiring every component to run on a GPU.

blocks.text: An experienced engineer can begin with the chapters on deadlines, consistency, idempotency, or incident response, but should return to the architecture chapters before implementing the capstone. A distributed system’s difficult defects often begin as an unstated local assumption: a callback that outlives its buffer, an error code that implies too much, or a database transaction that accidentally holds a lock while waiting on a remote service.

topics.title: Technical baseline
topics.summary: The executable companion uses C++20, CMake 3.24 or later, Linux sockets, the installed SQLite development library, and Python 3 for process-level tests. Linux is an intentional target for the transport exercises. The C++ standard does not define POSIX sockets, poll, or SQLite; their behavior must not be mistaken for portable language guarantees. The code does not download dependencies during configuration. See the included build report for the compiler, standard-library, operating-system, and SQLite versions actually exercised.

topics.title: What the companion actually contains
topics.summary: Each of the 28 chapters has a distinct executable demonstration. Some demonstrations are deliberately small policy models; others exercise real sockets or SQLite. The difference is stated in the chapter. A model that shows how a fencing check rejects an old token is not a consensus implementation. A permutation test of a small inbox model is not an exhaustive verification of an arbitrary network. An in-memory database exercises transactions without establishing crash durability; separate process and file-backed tests investigate restart behavior.

blocks.text: The integrated application contains three Linux executables: harbor_gateway, harbor_worker, and harbor_client. The gateway and worker run as separate processes and use separate SQLite database files. The gateway’s pending-job table acts as a durable outbox; the worker’s receipt table acts as an inbox and result record. The tests include lost acknowledgments, duplicate submissions, conflicting identities, fragmented input, an unavailable worker, restart recovery, and transaction rollback after a process is killed.

blocks.text: The supplied transport is IPv4 loopback-only and has no authentication or TLS. It is not a public server, a multiregion database, a complete Raft implementation, or a certified high-availability product. Chapters on security, replication, deployment, and operations explain what must be added and verified for those roles. Do not remove the loopback restriction and treat the teaching program as internet-ready infrastructure.

topics.title: Follow the evidence chain
topics.summary: Each chapter begins with a requirement or a failure that is easy to misinterpret. Numbered sections establish the underlying concepts; subsections develop the concrete decisions. A worked implementation exposes one mechanism. The failure clinic shows how a plausible shortcut breaks. The practice lab asks for a bounded change, an acceptance condition, and an explanation of the result. Solution notes describe why an answer satisfies the contract instead of merely giving a final number.

blocks.text: Keep four questions beside the editor: What changed? What became observable? Who may act on that observation? What remains uncertain? A client receiving a transport timeout has learned that it did not receive a timely answer. It has not necessarily learned that the worker did nothing. A successful COMMIT establishes a database-specific boundary under its durability assumptions. It does not prove that another database contains the same information. Thinking at the right boundary is the central skill of this book.

blocks.text: C++ tests use explicit checks rather than relying on assert, so Release builds do not silently remove their acceptance conditions. The Python integration harness requires ordinary nonoptimized interpreter execution and rejects -O or PYTHONOPTIMIZE modes that would remove its assertions. A zero test exit status means those conditions passed in that execution. It is not a guarantee of thread scheduling, power-loss durability, TLS policy, or performance on different hardware. Timing values in deterministic models are logical milliseconds supplied by the test, not measurements from a wall clock.

topics.title: Separate implementation from qualification
topics.summary: There are three levels of work in this volume. Mechanism laboratories isolate rules such as partial framing or cache invalidation. Integration laboratories run several real processes and persistent stores on a local machine. Production design exercises describe deployment, authentication, replication, migration, and operational evidence that cannot be inferred from a local loopback test. Moving between these levels requires additional validation; it is not accomplished by changing a heading from “lab” to “production.”

topics.summary: Chapters 1–4 establish architectural boundaries, APIs, and lifecycle. Chapters 5–9 move from asynchronous C++ execution into protocols, RPC, and discovery. Chapters 10–13 explain failure, consistency, coordination, and placement. Chapters 14–18 connect transactions, evolution, caches, messaging, and idempotency. Chapters 19–24 build resilience, security, observability, and testing. Chapters 25–28 assemble release, deployment, reliability, and the complete application.

blocks.text: A useful study rhythm is one chapter, one changed experiment, and one written argument. Predict the result before execution. Explain a failed prediction rather than editing the test until it passes. Keep reference implementations and previous test cases intact while adding a new mechanism. reading.title: Reading paths
paragraphs: Chapters 1–4 establish architectural boundaries, APIs, and lifecycle. Chapters 5–9 move from asynchronous C++ execution into protocols, RPC, and discovery. Chapters 19–24 build resilience, security, observability, and testing. Chapters 25–28 assemble release, deployment, reliability, and the complete application.
